chapters.title: AFTER THE FIRE
chapters.speech: In thirteenth-century Cairo, a medicine had to remain useful after the fire went out. That was a problem of process, material judgment, and trust.
chapters.source: al-Kūhīn al-ʿAṭṭār, original composition Cairo, 658 AH / 1260; historical synthesis in owner's accepted 2026 manuscript.

chapters.title: A WORKING HANDBOOK
chapters.speech: A pharmacist's handbook composed in Cairo in twelve sixty sets out practical rules. The manuscript pictured here is a later Egyptian copy, dated nineteen oh four.
chapters.source: Wellcome Collection MS Arabic 1002 (Egypt, 1904), Public Domain Mark; introductory scanned spreads in their original context.

chapters.title: THE BASE AND THE FORM
chapters.speech: Its rose-water and sugar base could become many different syrups. Fruit or medicinal material supplied the distinguishing form. The handbook describes this material relationship explicitly.
chapters.source: Minhāj al-dukkān syrup chapter; author's English translation of the julāb, hayūlā and ṣūra discussion.

chapters.title: MAKE, SKIM, STRAIN
chapters.tag: PROCESS IS PART OF THE PRODUCT
chapters.speech: Preparation demanded more than mixing. Sugar was dissolved, foam was removed, the liquid passed through cloth, and the vessel returned to the fire for further concentration.
chapters.source: Minhāj al-dukkān syrup chapter; process reconstruction from owner's accepted manuscript, pages 14–16.

chapters.title: KNOW THE CONSISTENCY
chapters.speech: A recognized consistency was the endpoint, not a numerical reading. Too little control risked spoilage. Pushing concentration too far could make a syrup crystallize.
chapters.source: Minhāj al-dukkān qiwām / ʿaqīd / mushāsh language; qualitative physical interpretation, no historic numerical assays.

chapters.title: WHAT IF IT FAILS?
chapters.speech: The handbook also described failure. Sugared syrup could be dissolved with warm water, brought back toward its intended consistency, and adjusted with fruit water.
chapters.source: Minhāj al-dukkān, end-of-syrup-chapter qawānīn and tasakkur repair instruction.

chapters.title: REPLACEMENT IS A JUDGMENT
chapters.speech: Scarcity raised another problem. The appropriate substitute had to be judged by function and preparation, not simply appearance. Deliberate adulteration posed a different kind of risk.
chapters.source: Minhāj al-dukkān substitution and ḥisba discussion; analytical distinction, no modern bioequivalence claim.

chapters.title: RECIPE IS NOT INVENTORY
chapters.speech: Cairo Genizah prescriptions illuminate the distance between written demand and available supply. Reliability was achieved through practical judgment, not through a medieval version of modern drug regulation.
chapters.source: Or.1081 J39 prescription as discussed in author's manuscript; actual Genizah fragment image NOT reproduced.
